# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and definition

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity characterised by delayed progression of injected contrast through the epicardial coronary arteries in the absence of significant obstructive disease. It is characterized by delayed progression of the injected contrast medium through the coronary tree, has been known to interventional cardiologists for approximately four decades, yet the pathogenic mechanisms remain unclear, and over 80% of patients experience recurrent chest pain resulting in considerable impairment of quality of life [1]. The condition was first described angiographically in 1972, when Tambe and colleagues reported angina pectoris and slow flow velocity of dye in coronary arteries as a new angiographic finding [2]. Beltrame later helped delineate CSFP as a discrete disorder; it is an angiographic finding characterized by delayed distal vessel opacification in the absence of significant epicardial coronary disease, and it has been speculated to be a new disease entity characterized by acute but recurrent perturbations of microvascular function [3].

## Diagnosis and quantification

Although early reports relied on subjective visual judgement and the semi-quantitative TIMI flow grade, the corrected TIMI frame count (CTFC) has become the reference standard. Because the TIMI flow grade is limited by its subjective and categorical nature, the number of cineframes needed for dye to reach standardized distal landmarks was counted to objectively assess an index of coronary blood flow as a continuous variable [4]. The method is reproducible, and in 78 consecutive normal arteries the left anterior descending (LAD) frame count (36.2 ± 2.6) was 1.7 times longer than the right coronary and circumflex counts, prompting division of the LAD count by 1.7 to derive the corrected value [4]. In clinical practice, CSFP is diagnosed when there is no epicardial obstruction and delayed distal filling with a TIMI frame count greater than 27, with the LAD value corrected by dividing by 1.7 [5]. Beltrame has also emphasised the importance of a standardised definition to distinguish CSFP from related entities [6].

## Epidemiology and clinical presentation

CSFP is encountered in roughly 1–7% of diagnostic angiograms. It is a frequent angiographic observation with a reported incidence of 1%–7% in patients undergoing diagnostic angiography, occurring most commonly in young men and smokers and in patients admitted with acute coronary syndrome [7]. In a large series, CSFP was identified in 5.5% of subjects referred for angiography, and was associated with male sex and obesity, with multivessel involvement potentially marking more diffuse disease [8]. The presentation is heterogeneous. CSFP is characterized by slow progression of angiographic contrast in the absence of epicardial stenosis, with a diverse presentation ranging from stable or unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, to vague chest discomfort [9]. Hypertension, dyslipidaemia and tobacco use are frequently identified independent associations. Acute coronary syndrome was the most common mode of presentation, and hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking and tobacco chewing were independent risk factors for CSFP [10].

## Pathophysiology

CSFP is now regarded as a manifestation of coronary microvascular dysfunction. Early histopathological work in patients with otherwise normal epicardial arteries showed improved flow after dipyridamole but not after intracoronary nitroglycerin, and endomyocardial biopsy frequently demonstrated wall thickening of microvessels with luminal narrowing [11]. Biopsy specimens have demonstrated small-vessel disease, cell edema, capillary damage, subclinical atherosclerosis, inflammation, fibromuscular hypertrophy and endothelial degeneration [12]. Functional studies support increased microvascular resistance. Among patients undergoing functional angiography, those with CSFP had lower flow velocity and higher microvascular resistance at rest than patients without CSFP [13]. Endothelial dysfunction is a central mechanism. Plasma nitric oxide levels are lower in patients with slow coronary flow than in controls, supporting a role in pathogenesis [14]. Endothelial function assessed by endothelin-1 and nitric oxide concentrations, and its response to exercise, is abnormal in slow-flow patients compared with healthy subjects [15]. Increased plasma endothelin-1, decreased nitric oxide and diffuse atherosclerosis may also reduce heart rate variability, implicating autonomic imbalance [16]. Reduced circulating endothelial nitric oxide synthase further supports endothelial dysfunction in the pathogenesis of slow coronary flow [17]. A genetic contribution has been proposed, since the allelic distribution of eNOS 894G/T was significantly associated with CSFP [18]. Metabolic derangements are common; patients with CSFP have higher total and LDL cholesterol, higher body mass index and a higher prevalence of metabolic syndrome [19].

## Inflammation and haematological factors

Systemic inflammation appears closely linked to CSFP. Meta-analysis indicates that systemic inflammation plays a significant role in the development of CSF, with a significant association between CSF and hs-CRP [20]. In diabetic patients, body mass index, haematocrit, neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and CRP correlate with CSF in poorly controlled diabetes, supporting a link between endothelial dysfunction and inflammation [21]. Oxidative stress is also implicated, since baseline malondialdehyde was increased and superoxide dismutase, catalase and nitric oxide were decreased in slow-flow patients [22].

## Treatment

No universally accepted therapy exists, and management is largely empirical. Calcium channel blockade is most established. Diagnosis was confirmed by an initial CTFC >27 frames that improved to <27 frames after intracoronary nifedipine, supporting a microvascular vasodilatory response [23]. The strongest randomised data involve mibefradil. Without changing epicardial diameter or rate-pressure product, mibefradil reduced the number of vessels exhibiting TIMI-2 flow and reduced total angina frequency by 56%, prolonged angina by 74% and nitrate consumption by 59%, while improving physical quality of life [24]. Microvascular dilators such as dipyridamole have shown angiographic benefit; oral dipyridamole, which dilates coronary microvessels, proved to be an effective treatment in most patients with slow coronary artery flow [25]. Statins and beta-blockers with vasodilatory properties have also been studied. In one trial, 97 patients with CSFP received simvastatin 40 mg daily for six months with perfusion imaging and lipid measurements at baseline and follow-up [26]. Nebivolol improves endothelial markers; after six months of nebivolol, all oxidative stress parameters improved significantly and approximated control values [22]. Newer agents continue to be explored: alprostadil was more effective in ameliorating angina symptoms in CSFP patients than isosorbide dinitrate [27].

## Prognosis

Long-term outcome data remain limited and conflicting. Some investigators have reported a favorable long-term prognosis, while others following patients over an average of 15 years concluded that CSFP is associated with a worse cardiac prognosis [28]. In one cohort, 1.2% of patients died, with death attributed to cardiac cause (sudden cardiac death) in three patients [29]. Medication adherence appears prognostically important; the most important factor determining cardiovascular death in patients with slow flow was discontinuation of medications, suggesting that treatment and follow-up should be equivalent to that of patients with coronary artery disease [30].

## Conclusion

CSFP is an under-recognised but clinically meaningful disorder of the coronary microcirculation, best quantified by the corrected TIMI frame count and increasingly understood as a syndrome of endothelial dysfunction, inflammation and increased microvascular resistance. Although calcium channel blockers, dipyridamole, statins and nebivolol show promise, robust, adequately powered trials and prospective outcome studies are still needed to standardise diagnosis, clarify prognosis, and define optimal therapy.
